corrected_value.title_o: Online social network size is reflected in human brain structure

decisions.quote:
Replication 2: Kanai et al. (2012)

Kanai et al. (2012) showed that individual differences in the
number of Facebook friends (FBN) and real-world social
network size (SNS) are positively correlated with GM volume
in several brain areas. The original authors replicated their
effects in an independent data set. In line with the original
authors' theorizing and results, we hypothesized positive
correlations between FBN and GM volume in left MTG, right
STS, right EC, and bilateral amygdala. In addition, we hypothesized a positive correlation between SNS and GM volume in right amygdala.
decisions.reason: Shipped row 1851 and blind target 1 both identify the same tested original study by Kanai, Bahrami, Roylance, and Rees ('Online social network size is reflected in human brain structure', DOI 10.1098/rspb.2011.1959, published online in 2011 and in print in 2012, tested as Replication 2), which is distinct from Replication 4 (Kanai, Dong, Bahrami, & Rees, 2011, blind target 3).

decisions.quote:
The five studies we attempted to replicate contained a total of 17 SBB correlations. The results from our
confirmatory analyses show that we were unable to successfully replicate any of these 17 correlations. For all but one
of the 17 findings under scrutiny, Bayesian hypothesis tests
indicated evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings agree on 'failed'. Under Codebook Rule 1 and the multi-original set rule, the authors' explicit overall verdict on their preregistered confirmatory analyses—that they were unable to successfully replicate any of the 17 correlations across the five studies—governs over the single unpreregistered exploratory correlation comparison (SNS and right amygdala GM volume) in Replication 2.

decisions.quote:
36 undergraduate psychology students (mean age ¼ 20.12,
SD ¼ 1.73; 18 females) with normal or corrected-to-normal
vision were recruited from the participant pool of a previous
43-participant MRI study. The MRI study was recently conducted by Forstmann and Wagenmakers' research group at
the University of Amsterdam and featured extensive Diffusion
Weighted Imaging (DWI) and T1-weighted imaging. Hence,
the additional effort involved in replicating the five studies
consisted primarily in having participants complete a battery
of behavioral tests.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings agree on 'replication'. The authors collected new behavioral and neuroimaging data from an independent sample of 36 undergraduate students to re-test the published structural brain-behavior correlation findings of Kanai, Bahrami, Roylance, and Rees (2012).

corrected_value.title: Cortico-striatal connections predict control over speed and accuracy in perceptual decision making.

decisions.location: Section 2.2.1 (Methods, pp. 120-121), Section 3.1 (Results, p. 123, lines 1017-1036), and References (p. 132, lines 2331-2336)
decisions.quote:
Replication 1: Forstmann et al. (2010)

Forstmann et al. (2010) reported that individual differences in
tract strength from right pre-SMA to right striatum predict
individual differences in control over speed and accuracy in a
perceptual decision making paradigm. The original authors
replicated their effect in an independent data set. In line with
the original authors' theorizing and results, we hypothesized
the presence of a positive correlation between pre-SMAstriatum tract strength and LBA flexibility.
Three participants did not complete the behavioral task
and were thus excluded from further analysis. Tract strengths
of 2 out of 33 participants deviated more than 2.5 SDs from the
group mean, and were thus excluded from this replication
attempt. After outlier rejection, tract strength data ranged
from .682 to .914, with a mean of .819 and a standard deviation
of .061. LBA flexibility ranged from .020 to 1.554, with a mean
of .578 and a standard deviation of .410. A one-sided Bayesian
hypothesis test for positive correlations was performed on
these data. Its result is shown in Table 2 and Fig. 3. The Bayes
factor shows that there is moderate support for the null hypothesis of no correlation.
decisions.reason: In Replication 1 (Sections 2.2.1 and 3.1), Boekel et al. (2015) empirically re-test Forstmann et al. (2010; PNAS, 107(36), 15916-15920) in an independent sample (n = 31 after exclusions), testing whether probabilistic tractography white-matter tract strength between right pre-SMA and right striatum positively correlates with LBA response-caution flexibility in the random dot motion task (finding r = .03, BF01 = 3.90). The only supplied shipped row (input_row_index 1851, Kanai et al., 2011/2012, 10.1098/rspb.2011.1959) corresponds to Replication 2 (sibling target_index 1) on social network size and grey-matter volume, and sibling targets 2, 3, and 4 re-test distinct original papers (Xu et al., 2012; Kanai, Dong, et al., 2011; Westlye et al., 2011). No prior adjudication or state file exists.

decisions.location: Section 2.2.3 (Methods, pp. 121-122), Section 3.3 (Results, p. 125, lines 1276-1295), and References (p. 133, lines 2543-2546)
decisions.quote:
Replication 3: Xu et al. (2012)

Xu et al. (2012) reported that individual differences in diffusion measures of several WM pathways are positively correlated with individual differences in the tendency to seek out
new potentially rewarding experiences (i.e., BAS-Fun) and the
sensitivity to signals of reward and non-punishment (BASTotal). In line with the original authors' theorizing and results,
we hypothesized a positive correlation between the BAS-Total
scores and l1 within left CR and left SLF, a positive correlation
between BAS-Fun and FA in left CR and SLF, a positive correlation between BAS-FUN and l1 in left CR and SLF, and a
positive correlation between BAS-Fun and MD in left ILF and
IFOF.
One participant was excluded from l1 analyses due to WM
structural measures deviating more than 2.5 SDs from the
group mean. After outlier rejection, the following summary
statistics describe our data: BAS-Total: range: 14e31, mean:
22.833, sd: 3.783. BAS-FUN: range: 5e12, mean: 7.667, sd: 1.821.
FA in left CR and SLF: range: .649e.810, mean: .736, sd: .039. l1
in left CR and SLF: range: 7.4E4 e 9.2E4, mean: 8.2E4, sd: 3.7E5.
MD in left SLF and IFOF: range: 3.9E4 e 4.7E4, mean: 4.3E4, sd:
1.8E5. One-sided Bayesian hypothesis tests for positive correlations were performed on these data.
decisions.reason: In Replication 3 (Sections 2.2.3 and 3.3), Boekel et al. (2015) empirically re-test Xu et al. (2012; Human Brain Mapping, 33(4), 994-1002) in a new sample (n = 35-36), testing four positive correlations between BIS/BAS Behavioral Activation System scores (BAS-Total and BAS-Fun) and white-matter DTI metrics (lambda_1, FA, and MD) in left CR/SLF and left ILF/IFOF ROIs (finding BF01 = 11.74, 9.40, 10.57, and 2.04 in favor of the null). The only supplied shipped row (input_row_index 1851, Kanai et al., 2011/2012, 10.1098/rspb.2011.1959) is Replication 2 on online social network size and VBM grey-matter volume, and sibling targets 0, 3, and 4 are independent original studies by different authors. No prior adjudication or state file exists.

corrected_value.authors: Kanai, R., Dong, M. Y., Bahrami, B., & Rees, G.
corrected_value.title: Distractibility in daily life is reflected in the structure and function of human parietal cortex.

decisions.location: Section 2.2.4 (Methods, p. 122), Section 3.4 (Results, p. 125, lines 1296-1309), and References (p. 132, lines 2396-2399)
decisions.quote:
Kanai, Dong, et al., (2011) reported that individual differences
in the degree of distractibility (CFQ) are correlated with GM
volume in several brain areas. In line with the original authors'
theorizing and results, we hypothesized a positive correlation
between CFQ scores and GM volume in left SPL, and a negative
correlation between CFQ and GM volumes in left mPFC.
The following summary statistics describe our data: CFQ:
range: 5e29, mean: 16.472, sd: 5.443. GM in left SPL: range:
.378e.812, mean: .545, sd: .113. GM in left mPFC: range:
.342e.693, mean: .499, sd: .101. Results of the one-sided
Bayesian hypothesis tests for correlations are shown in
Table 5 and Fig. 6. In both cases we find anecdotal support
(“not worth more than a bare mention”, Jeffreys, 1961,
Appendix B) for the null hypothesis.
decisions.reason: In Replication 4 (Sections 2.2.4 and 3.4), Boekel et al. (2015) empirically re-test Kanai, Dong, Bahrami, & Rees (2011; Journal of Neuroscience, 31(18), 6620-6626) in a new sample (n = 36), testing whether Cognitive Failures Questionnaire (CFQ) distractibility scores correlate positively with grey-matter volume in left superior parietal lobe (SPL) and negatively with grey-matter volume in left middle prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (finding r = .22, BF01 = 1.24 and r = -.19, BF01 = 1.51). Although overlapping in authors with shipped row 1851 (Kanai, Bahrami, Roylance, & Rees, 2011 online / 2012 print, 10.1098/rspb.2011.1959, Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 279, 1327-1334), shipped row 1851 is a different original study on online/real-world social network size and MTG/STS/EC/amygdala grey-matter volume (replicated separately as Replication 2, sibling target_index 1). Sibling targets 0, 2, and 4 also re-test distinct original papers. No prior adjudication or state file exists.

decisions.location: Section 2.2.5 (Methods, pp. 122-123), Section 3.5 (Results, p. 126, lines 1525-1535), and References (p. 133, lines 2529-2532)
decisions.quote:
Replication 5: Westlye et al., 2011

Westlye et al. (2011) reported that individual differences in
aspects of attention (executive control and alerting) are
correlated with cortical thickness in several brain areas. In
line with the original authors' theorizing and results, we hypothesized negative correlations between executive control
scores and CT in left caudal ACC, left STG, and right MTG. In
addition, we hypothesized a negative correlation between
alerting scores and CT in left SPL.
One participant was excluded due to cortical thickness
measures deviating more than 2.5 SDs from the group mean.
decisions.reason: In Replication 5 (Sections 2.2.5 and 3.5), Boekel et al. (2015) empirically re-test Westlye, Grydeland, Walhovd, & Fjell (2011; Cerebral Cortex, 21(2), 345-356) in a new sample (n = 35), testing four negative correlations between Attention Network Test (ANT) executive control and alerting scores and FreeSurfer cortical thickness in left caudal ACC, left STG, right MTG, and left SPL (finding BF01 = 1.71, 2.23, 1.60, and 8.58 in favor of the null). The only supplied shipped row (input_row_index 1851, Kanai et al., 2011/2012, 10.1098/rspb.2011.1959) is Replication 2 on social network size and VBM grey-matter volume, and sibling targets 0, 2, and 3 re-test distinct original studies by other authors. No prior adjudication or state file exists.
